items.stem: Which equation says exactly the same thing as $\log_{3}(x) = 4$?
items.hint: A logarithm is an exponent, so read the equation aloud as the base raised to the answer gives the argument.
worked: Name the parts: the base is $3$, the value of the log is $4$, and the argument is $x$.
Base raised to that value gives the argument: $3^{4} = x$.

items.hint: Rewrite $32$ as a power of $2$ so that both sides of the equation have the same base.
worked: Write the right side with base $2$: $32 = 2^{5}$.

items.hint: Combine the left side into a single logarithm first, then remember that every log argument must stay positive.
worked: The value $x = -4$ makes $\log_{2}(x)$ undefined, so the only solution is $x = 2$.

items.stem: A student solves $\log_{2}(x+3) - \log_{2}(x-3) = 2$ in three lines. Line 1: $\log_{2}\left(\dfrac{x+3}{x-3}\right) = 2$. Line 2: $\dfrac{x+3}{x-3} = 4$. Line 3: $x + 3 = 4x - 12$, so $x = 5$. Which statement about this work is true?
items.hint: Test each line on its own: which rule turns a difference of logs into one log, and which number gets raised to the power $2$?
worked: Line 1 uses the quotient rule correctly: a difference of logs is the log of a quotient.
Line 2 converts to exponential form using the base $2$, and $2^{2} = 4$, so it is right.
Domain check: at $x = 5$ the arguments are $8$ and $2$, both positive, so the work is correct.

options.text: Line 1 is wrong: the left side equals $\log_{2}\left((x+3)-(x-3)\right) = \log_{2}(6)$, so the equation has no solution.
Line 1 is wrong: the left side should be written as $\dfrac{\log_{2}(x+3)}{\log_{2}(x-3)}$.
Line 2 is wrong: it should say $\dfrac{x+3}{x-3} = 10^{2}$.
The work is correct: $x = 5$, and both log arguments are positive there.

items.hint: Convert to exponential form first, then ask how many real numbers square to that result and whether each one leaves the argument positive.
worked: A squared quantity has two real square roots: $x = 8$ or $x = -8$.
Check $x = -8$: the argument is $(-8)^{2} = 64$, which is positive, and $\log_{2}(64) = 6$.
Both values satisfy the original equation, so $x = \pm 8$.
